Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

---search help---
Find the code for a task from a plain-language query (start here)

Usage:
  entire graph search --query "issue or concept" --repo . [--top-k 10] [--format text|json|ndjson|agent] [--head] [--profile fast|full] [--deep]

Ranked source regions for a plain-language description, with source and file:line inline, budgeted to drop straight into context. This is the first move for almost every locate task.

By default search returns: ranked candidate fix sites (top hits as full function bodies), RELATED SITES, the COVERING TEST plus other tests over the same code (ALSO COVERING), SAME-CONCEPT LITERAL (every place the concept is named, tagged EDIT/CONSUMER/DOC), a VERIFY line (the narrowest test command for the file), and a CLOSED-SET WARNING when a switch over a sealed set would fail at runtime. The three reference blocks (container map, signature types, declaration card) are OFF by default because they cost turns in agent sessions; --reference-blocks all turns them on for interactive reading.

--top-k only changes how many results come back; --deep additionally runs the exhaustive sparse (BM25) pass and fuses it with the semantic ranking (slower, reads every eligible file).

Ranking returns one region per unit, which is right for code and wrong for whole prose documents: one markdown document can hold the answer across several distant regions. So for prose the unit is the SECTION, not the file — a document's headed sections are ranked against every other section on their own scores, exactly as independent files would be (--document-resolution ranks a document as one unit instead). Separately, and on prose of any shape including headed documents, when fewer distinct units match than --top-k asked for, the spare slots are spent returning finer regions of the same document as results of their own (multi-resolution retrieval) — strictly additive, so it never displaces a unit and never breaches --max-context-bytes. --single-resolution turns that off. The two stack: a headed document can be ranked by section AND have spare slots filled with promoted passages, so a prose payload may carry both.

Flags:
  --query <text>            The task or bug in one plain sentence (required)
  --repo <path>             Repository to search (default: current repo)
  --top-k <n>               Number of results to return (default: 10)
  --format text|json|ndjson|agent
                            Output format; text is tiered for reading, agent is compact (default: json)
  --head                    Search the committed tree (cached) instead of the working tree
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth; use full for bug-fix/locate (call-graph active) (default: fast)
  --deep                    Also run the exhaustive BM25 pass and fuse it (slower)
  --single-resolution       One result per ranked unit; do not spend spare slots on finer regions of a prose document
  --document-resolution     Rank a prose document as one unit; do not rank its sections separately
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Output byte budget; 0 = unbounded (default: 24576)
  --reference-blocks all|container-map,signature-types,type-card
                            Turn reference blocks back on (off by default)
  --max-indexed-files <n>   Bound cold-search parsing to N files
  --index-all-files         Widen cold-search parsing to every file
  --cache-dir <path>        Override the committed-tree cache directory
  --no-cache                Disable the committed-tree cache

Examples:
  entire graph search --repo . --query "token refresh returns 401" --format text --top-k 8
  entire graph search --repo . --query "csv export ordering" --profile full

Usage:
  entire graph impact --symbol NAME|<file>:<line> --repo . [--depth 1|2] [--limit 15] [--format text|json]

Everything the graph knows about changing one symbol in a single bounded explanation: direct + transitive callers (depth <=2), callees, type consumers (USES_TYPE/PARAM_TYPE/RETURNS_TYPE), data flows, files that historically co-change with the symbol's file, and same-container siblings. Run this before changing a function/type's behavior.

Ambiguous names return the definition list; rerun with --file/--line/--kind (or --symbol <file>:<line>) to pick one.

  --repo <path>             Repository (default: current repo)
  --file <path>             Disambiguate an ambiguous name by file
  --line <n>                Disambiguate by line
  --kind <kind>             Disambiguate by symbol kind
  --depth 1|2               Caller-traversal depth (default: 2)
  --limit <n>               Max entries per section (default: 15)
  --format text|json        Output format
  --max-context-bytes <n>   Total text budget (default: 4096)
  --exclude-tests           Drop test-only entries
  --head                    Query the committed tree (cached)
  --profile syntax-only|fast|full
                            Parsing depth (default: full)

Examples:
  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol WriteText

9. File creation and ownership rule — LOCKED
Do not mechanically create every file in the repository tree or add extra abstractions merely because they were planned. The repository tree defines the intended baseline and architectural direction; implementation should create, split, merge, move, or omit files only when the actual working code genuinely requires it.

• Keep each file focused on one clear dominant responsibility.
• Preserve the locked client/server/shared separation and adapter/core boundaries wherever practical.
• Avoid speculative abstractions, empty placeholder files, generic dumping-ground modules, and unnecessary file/folder proliferation.
• Prefer the simplest file structure that keeps the implementation understandable, testable where valuable, and fast to navigate for a fresh agent.
• Use engineering judgment on the fly based on the full blueprint and current implementation state rather than following filenames mechanically.
• If a meaningful structural deviation from the planned repository tree becomes necessary, explain the reason and expected impact to the user before making it, obtain approval, and record the accepted deviation in the living execution docs where appropriate.

The goal is disciplined ownership without duplicating a large file-by-file specification that the implementing agent can infer from the locked architecture, repository tree, contracts, and current code.

10. Data contracts — LOCKED
Section 10 defines only the shared data shapes needed so Entire, Databricks, AgentRouter, deterministic backend logic, persistence, API, and React can exchange information without guessing each other’s format.

Core rules
• Raw Entire, Databricks, and AgentRouter response shapes stay inside their adapters. The rest of the app uses our own canonical contracts.
• Keep the contract set small. Create a formal contract only when data crosses an architectural boundary, is persisted/shared with the frontend, or must be runtime-validated for trust.
• Use Zod schemas in `src/shared/contracts.ts` as the source definitions and infer TypeScript types from them. Do not maintain duplicate interfaces/schemas or create types for every internal variable.

Canonical contract set
• `CheckpointSummary` — lightweight checkpoint data needed by the Decision Timeline.
• `CheckpointEvidenceBundle` / `Evidence` — normalized Entire-derived evidence for a checkpoint. Evidence must retain stable deterministic identity and provenance.
• `EvidenceRetrievalHit` — Databricks search reference/ranking metadata. A hit is not trusted evidence by itself; it must resolve back to canonical Entire-derived evidence before use.
• `IntentSignal` / `SemanticAnalysis` — structured GPT output for intent/implementation judgment using Done / Missing / Drifted / Risky plus evidence references.
• `IntentGuardScore` — deterministic score/summary derived from validated signals; the exact formula belongs to Section 13.
• `HandoffBrief` — fresh-agent continuation data: intent, completed/missing work, risks, next step, evidence, and optional relevant prior context when Databricks retrieval genuinely adds useful history.
• `ReviewResult` — the single validated product result returned to the UI.
• `PersistedReviewRecord` — cache/versioning envelope around a validated review.
• `ApiError` — one small shared error shape for backend stages.

Trust boundary
Evidence IDs/provenance are deterministic and must never be invented by GPT or Databricks. Any model-returned evidence reference or Databricks retrieval hit must resolve to known canonical evidence before it can support a trusted signal, score, handoff, or UI drill-down.

Deferred details
Do not over-specify field-by-field shapes here. Implement the minimum fields genuinely required by the working product. Entire-dependent fields are finalized after Section 11 verifies the actual CLI data; the scoring formula is finalized in Section 13; exact Databricks table/index/search/filter details are finalized in Section 14.

Success condition: the whole application speaks one small trusted internal vocabulary without provider-specific shapes leaking across boundaries or speculative schema complexity.

11. Entire Checkpoint ingestion contract — LOCKED
V1 uses the Entire CLI as the only checkpoint-ingestion boundary; do not read Entire’s internal refs/metadata files directly.
• Timeline: `entire checkpoint list --json` → normalize committed/condensed current-branch checkpoints into `CheckpointSummary[]`.
• Selected checkpoint: `entire checkpoint explain <id> --json` for metadata plus `--transcript` for transcript content; use `--raw-transcript` only when needed as fallback. If multiple sessions contributed, retrieve the needed session transcript(s) through the CLI rather than assuming one session.
• `entire checkpoint list --pending --json` is outside pre-noon V1 and remains a Curveball/extension option.
• The Entire adapter validates command success/output and immediately normalizes raw data into the Section 10 contracts; raw Entire shapes do not escape the adapter.
• Missing optional fields stay absent; never fabricate them. Non-zero exit, malformed JSON/output, or unavailable checkpoint/transcript must surface as explicit ingestion errors.
• Before implementation/demo, capture small real CLI fixtures for list + selected-checkpoint data and confirm the installed Entire version supports the required commands.
Success condition: startup can populate the timeline and checkpoint selection can produce normalized evidence without depending on Entire’s internal storage implementation.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for the resume view instead: live checkpoints on
the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed), plus logs-only resume points
recovered from commits whose logs are already condensed.

Output modes:

  --pending          Select the pending dataset: live shadow-branch
                     checkpoints plus logs-only resume points.

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending).

  entire checkpoint list [flags]

      --no-pager         Disable pager output

docs/architecture\ref-checkpoint-backend.md:51:- A **ULID**'s leading chars encode a millisecond timestamp (barely varying between nearby checkpoints) while its trailing chars are random — so sharding on the suffix keeps buckets even *and* keeps the ID itself lexicographically time-sortable.
docs/architecture\ref-checkpoint-backend.md:129:- Each advertised ref that has no local ref yet is added to the result as a not-yet-hydrated `CheckpointInfo`. Its `CreatedAt` is recovered from the ULID timestamp in the ref name, so it sorts by real recency without a fetch; the rest of its contents are **hydrated lazily on the next read** via the on-demand ref fetch (and, on the branch `explain` / `checkpoint list` path, eagerly for the truncated display set so `--session` filters see real SessionIDs).

docs/architecture\agent-guide.md:577:Pi uses JSONL (one JSON object per line) with a tree-shaped entry model. Every entry has `id` and optional `parentId`, enabling Pi's `/fork` and `/clone` branching. Each entry has `type` (`"message"` for conversational entries), `timestamp`, and (for message entries) a `message` object with `role`, `content`, and optional `usage`:

docs/architecture\agent-guide.md:732:Pi extension hooks fire via `execFile` (non-blocking) to avoid blocking the agent. The extension listens for Pi lifecycle events (`session_start`, `before_agent_start`, `agent_end`, `session_shutdown`) and dispatches each to `entire hooks pi <event>` with a JSON payload containing `type`, `cwd`, `session_file`, `session_id`, and (for `before_agent_start`) `prompt`.

---local_cli---
List checkpoints on the current branch.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for the resume view instead: live checkpoints on
the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed), plus logs-only resume points
recovered from commits whose logs are already condensed.

Output modes:
  --json             Machine-readable JSON instead of the human view.
  --pending          Select the pending dataset: live shadow-branch
                     checkpoints plus logs-only resume points.
  --pending --json   Pending checkpoints as JSON (replaces the deprecated rewind --list).

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending).

Usage:
  entire checkpoint list [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for list
      --json             Output as JSON instead of the human view
      --no-pager         Disable pager output
      --pending          List pending checkpoints — live shadow-branch state plus logs-only resume points
      --session string   Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

Entity-level change list between two refs

Usage:
  entire graph diff --base <rev> --head <rev> [--json] [--progress] [--max-seconds n] [--repo path] [-- path...]

Entity-level change list between two refs, with heuristic dependent counts. High dependent counts on a signature change mean run tests first. `analyze` is an alias for this command. Stops cleanly after --max-seconds and emits the partial result with W_ANALYSIS_BUDGET_EXCEEDED warnings.

Flags:
  --base <rev>        Base revision (default: HEAD~1)
  --head <rev>        Head revision (default: HEAD)
  --json              Emit the result as JSON
  --progress          Emit progress events to stderr
  --max-seconds <n>   Analysis budget; 0 = unlimited (default: 120)
  --repo <path>       Repository (default: current repo)

Examples:
  entire graph diff --base main --head HEAD --json

- Raw transcript bytes remain local.
- External evidence projections exclude prompt/transcript evidence.
- Incomplete context is always `provisional`.
- Incomplete reviews cannot contain an Intent Guard score.
- UI labels `Complete`, `Incomplete`, and `Not assessed`.
- Added a redacted/missing fixture and focused tests.
- Entire Graph search and pre-change impact analysis completed locally with no egress.

You can create an AI Search index using the UI, the Python SDK, or the REST API. The UI is the simplest approach.

There are two types of indexes:

  * Delta Sync Index automatically syncs with a source Delta Table, automatically and incrementally updating the index as the underlying data in the Delta Table changes.
  * Direct Vector Access Index supports direct read and write of vectors and metadata. The user is responsible for updating this table using the REST API or the Python SDK. This type of index cannot be created using the UI. You must use the REST API or the SDK.

Delta Sync Indexes support the following search modes:

  * Vector search (ANN or hybrid): Requires embedding columns. Supports both standard and storage-optimized endpoints. You can also use `query_type="FULL_TEXT"` for keyword search on these indexes.
  * Dedicated full-text search index (Beta): A Delta Sync Index created without any embedding columns, for keyword-only search. Available only on storage-optimized endpoints using triggered sync mode. See Create a full-text search index.

note

The column name `_id` is reserved. If your source table has a column named `_id`, rename it before creating an AI Search index.

### Create index using the UI​

  1. In the left sidebar, click Catalog to open the Catalog Explorer UI.

  2. Navigate to the Delta table you want to use.

  3. Click the Create button at the upper-right, and select Vector search index from the drop-down menu.

Image: Create index button

  4. Use the selectors in the dialog to configure the index.

Image: create index dialog

## Update an AI Search index​

### Update a Delta Sync Index​

Indexes created with Continuous sync mode automatically update when the source Delta table changes. If you are using Triggered sync mode, you can start the sync using the UI, the Python SDK, or the REST API.

  * Databricks UI
  * Python SDK
  * REST API

  1. In Catalog Explorer, navigate to the AI Search index.

  2. On the Overview tab, in the Data Ingest section, click Sync now.

Image: Sync now button to sync an AI Search index from Catalog Explorer..

For details, see the Python SDK reference.

Python
    
    `client = AISearchClient()
    index = client.get_index(index_name="vector_search_demo.vector_search.en_wiki_index")
    index.sync()
    `

See the REST API reference documentation: POST /api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/{index_name}/sync.

### Update a Direct Vector Access Index​

You can use the Python SDK or the REST API to insert, update, or delete data from a Direct Vector Access Index.

  * Python SDK
  * REST API

For details, see the Python SDK reference.

Python
    
    `index.upsert([
        {
            "id": 1,
            "field2": "value2",
            "field3": 3.0,
            "text_vector": [1.0] * 1024
        },
        {
            "id": 2,
            "field2": "value2",
            "field3": 3.0,
            "text_vector": [1.1] * 1024
        }
    ])
    `

See the REST API reference documentation: POST /api/2.0/vector-search/indexes.

For production applications, Databricks recommends using service principals instead of personal access tokens. Performance can be improved by up to 100 msec per query.

The following code example illustrates how to update an index using a service principal.

sh
    
    `export SP_CLIENT_ID=...
    export SP_CLIENT_SECRET=...
    export INDEX_NAME=...
    export WORKSPACE_URL=https://...
    export WORKSPACE_ID=...
    # Set authorization details to generate OAuth token
    export AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS='{"type":"unity_catalog_permission","securable_type":"table","securable_object_name":"'"$INDEX_NAME"'","operation": "WriteVectorIndex"}'
    # Generate OAuth token
    export TOKEN=$(curl -X POST --url $WORKSPACE_URL/oidc/v1/token -u "$SP_CLIENT_ID:$SP_CLIENT_SECRET" --data 'grant_type=client_credentials' --data 'scope=all-apis' --data-urlencode 'authorization_details=['"$AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS"']' | jq .access_token | tr -d '"')
    # Get index URL
    export INDEX_URL=$(curl -X GET -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME | jq -r '.status.index_url' | tr -d '"')
    # Upsert data into AI Search index.
    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url https://$INDEX_URL/upsert-data --data '{"inputs_json": "[...]"}'
    # Delete data from AI Search index
    curl -X DELETE -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url https://$INDEX_URL/delete-data --data '{"primary_keys": [...]}'
    `

The following code example illustrates how to update an index using a personal access token (PAT).

sh
    
    `export TOKEN=...
    export INDEX_NAME=...
    export WORKSPACE_URL=https://...
    # Upsert data into AI Search index.
    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME/upsert-data --data '{"inputs_json": "..."}'
    # Delete data from AI Search index
    curl -X DELETE -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME/delete-data --data '{"primary_keys": [...]}'
    `

### How to make schema changes with no downtime​

Schema changes to the source table are not supported unless you rebuild the index. This includes modifying existing columns and adding new columns. The index schema is fixed at creation time, so any schema changes require creating a new index to take effect.

Follow these steps to rebuild and deploy the index with no downtime:

  1. Perform the schema change on your source table.
  2. Create a new index using the updated schema.
  3. After the new index is ready, switch traffic to the new index.
  4. Delete the original index.

## databricks vector-search-indexes upsert-data-vector-index​

Upsert data into an index.
    
    `databricks vector-search-indexes upsert-data-vector-index INDEX_NAME INPUTS_JSON [flags]
    `

#### Arguments​

`INDEX_NAME`

    Name of the vector index where data is to be upserted. Must be a Direct Vector Access Index.

`INPUTS_JSON`

    JSON string representing the data to be upserted

#### Options​

`--json JSON`

    The inline JSON string or the @path to the JSON file with the request body.

Global flags

#### Examples​

The following example upserts data into a Direct Vector Access index:

Bash
    
    `databricks vector-search-indexes upsert-data-vector-index my-index '{"vectors": [{"id": "1", "vector": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], "metadata": {"title": "Document 1"}}]}'
    `

## Global flags​

`--debug`

  Whether to enable debug logging.

`-h` or `--help`

    Display help for the Databricks CLI or the related command group or the related command.

`--log-file` string

    A string representing the file to write output logs to. If this flag is not specified then the default is to write output logs to stderr.

`--log-format` format

    The log format type, `text` or `json`. The default value is `text`.

`--log-level` string

    A string representing the log format level. If not specified then the log format level is disabled.

`-o, --output` type

    The command output type, `text` or `json`. The default value is `text`.

`-p, --profile` string

    The name of the profile in the `~/.databrickscfg` file to use to run the command. If this flag is not specified then if it exists, the profile named `DEFAULT` is used.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Product

## Noon Curveball

The product must support sensitive repositories. Raw prompts and transcripts stay local and are never included in a Databricks or other external-service request. Redacted, unavailable, and partial fields remain useful through bounded local file, test, summary, and provenance evidence.

Incomplete context is a first-class state. It must always render as provisional, must not receive an Intent Guard score, and must tell the user what is missing and what to verify next.

## Current architecture

React UI -> Express API -> Entire CLI or explicit fixture source -> canonical evidence bundle -> privacy projection -> Databricks retrieval when configured or explicit local fallback -> deterministic local review and handoff.

Databricks may receive only evidence marked `shareable`. Every returned hit must match a canonical local evidence ID, Checkpoint ID, and content hash before use. Raw provider shapes remain inside their adapters.

## Current constraint

The official redacted attachment is not present in the workspace. A representative redacted/missing fixture is included for implementation and focused verification until the official fixture is available.

# DECISIONS.md

Status: LIVING DECISION LOG - append meaningful decisions only.

## D-015 - Sensitive Checkpoint boundary

Raw prompt and transcript content is local-only. External services receive only an allowlisted projection of canonical evidence explicitly marked `shareable`. The projection omits the raw context fields by construction.

Incomplete Checkpoint context produces a provisional result with no score. This is enforced in the shared Zod contract so server, persistence, API, and UI cannot silently relabel an incomplete result as complete or authoritative.

## D-016 - Privacy-safe Databricks retrieval

Databricks remains the optional semantic retrieval layer, but the Curveball narrows its input to shareable structural evidence. Query hits are references only and must resolve to canonical local evidence by evidence ID, Checkpoint ID, and content hash. Missing configuration, service failure, or invalid hits falls back explicitly to local evidence.

Delta Sync is triggered through the configured index. The application does not upload prompt or transcript records during synchronization.

Status: LIVING - active material risks only.

Mitigation: keep the projection as the only external input builder, retain schema/runtime validation, and cover redacted, missing, and raw-secret cases with focused tests.

Impact: fixture loading or completeness detection may fail during judging.

9. File creation and ownership rule — LOCKED
Do not mechanically create every file in the repository tree or add extra abstractions merely because they were planned. The repository tree defines the intended baseline and architectural direction; implementation should create, split, merge, move, or omit files only when the actual working code genuinely requires it.

• Keep each file focused on one clear dominant responsibility.
• Preserve the locked client/server/shared separation and adapter/core boundaries wherever practical.
• Avoid speculative abstractions, empty placeholder files, generic dumping-ground modules, and unnecessary file/folder proliferation.
• Prefer the simplest file structure that keeps the implementation understandable, testable where valuable, and fast to navigate for a fresh agent.
• Use engineering judgment on the fly based on the full blueprint and current implementation state rather than following filenames mechanically.
• If a meaningful structural deviation from the planned repository tree becomes necessary, explain the reason and expected impact to the user before making it, obtain approval, and record the accepted deviation in the living execution docs where appropriate.

The goal is disciplined ownership without duplicating a large file-by-file specification that the implementing agent can infer from the locked architecture, repository tree, contracts, and current code.

10. Data contracts — LOCKED
Section 10 defines only the shared data shapes needed so Entire, Databricks, AgentRouter, deterministic backend logic, persistence, API, and React can exchange information without guessing each other’s format.

Core rules
• Raw Entire, Databricks, and AgentRouter response shapes stay inside their adapters. The rest of the app uses our own canonical contracts.
• Keep the contract set small. Create a formal contract only when data crosses an architectural boundary, is persisted/shared with the frontend, or must be runtime-validated for trust.
• Use Zod schemas in `src/shared/contracts.ts` as the source definitions and infer TypeScript types from them. Do not maintain duplicate interfaces/schemas or create types for every internal variable.

Canonical contract set
• `CheckpointSummary` — lightweight checkpoint data needed by the Decision Timeline.
• `CheckpointEvidenceBundle` / `Evidence` — normalized Entire-derived evidence for a checkpoint. Evidence must retain stable deterministic identity and provenance.
• `EvidenceRetrievalHit` — Databricks search reference/ranking metadata. A hit is not trusted evidence by itself; it must resolve back to canonical Entire-derived evidence before use.
• `IntentSignal` / `SemanticAnalysis` — structured GPT output for intent/implementation judgment using Done / Missing / Drifted / Risky plus evidence references.
• `IntentGuardScore` — deterministic score/summary derived from validated signals; the exact formula belongs to Section 13.
• `HandoffBrief` — fresh-agent continuation data: intent, completed/missing work, risks, next step, evidence, and optional relevant prior context when Databricks retrieval genuinely adds useful history.
• `ReviewResult` — the single validated product result returned to the UI.
• `PersistedReviewRecord` — cache/versioning envelope around a validated review.
• `ApiError` — one small shared error shape for backend stages.

Trust boundary
Evidence IDs/provenance are deterministic and must never be invented by GPT or Databricks. Any model-returned evidence reference or Databricks retrieval hit must resolve to known canonical evidence before it can support a trusted signal, score, handoff, or UI drill-down.

Deferred details
Do not over-specify field-by-field shapes here. Implement the minimum fields genuinely required by the working product. Entire-dependent fields are finalized after Section 11 verifies the actual CLI data; the scoring formula is finalized in Section 13; exact Databricks table/index/search/filter details are finalized in Section 14.

Success condition: the whole application speaks one small trusted internal vocabulary without provider-specific shapes leaking across boundaries or speculative schema complexity.

11. Entire Checkpoint ingestion contract — LOCKED
V1 uses the Entire CLI as the only checkpoint-ingestion boundary; do not read Entire’s internal refs/metadata files directly.
• Timeline: `entire checkpoint list --json` → normalize committed/condensed current-branch checkpoints into `CheckpointSummary[]`.
• Selected checkpoint: `entire checkpoint explain <id> --json` for metadata plus `--transcript` for transcript content; use `--raw-transcript` only when needed as fallback. If multiple sessions contributed, retrieve the needed session transcript(s) through the CLI rather than assuming one session.
• `entire checkpoint list --pending --json` is outside pre-noon V1 and remains a Curveball/extension option.
• The Entire adapter validates command success/output and immediately normalizes raw data into the Section 10 contracts; raw Entire shapes do not escape the adapter.
• Missing optional fields stay absent; never fabricate them. Non-zero exit, malformed JSON/output, or unavailable checkpoint/transcript must surface as explicit ingestion errors.
• Before implementation/demo, capture small real CLI fixtures for list + selected-checkpoint data and confirm the installed Entire version supports the required commands.
Success condition: startup can populate the timeline and checkpoint selection can produce normalized evidence without depending on Entire’s internal storage implementation.

List checkpoints on the current branch.

By default shows condensed checkpoints from the checkpoints branch for the
current branch. Use --pending for the resume view instead: live checkpoints on
the session's shadow branch (not yet condensed), plus logs-only resume points
recovered from commits whose logs are already condensed.

Output modes:
  --json             Machine-readable JSON instead of the human view.
  --pending          Select the pending dataset: live shadow-branch
                     checkpoints plus logs-only resume points.
  --pending --json   Pending checkpoints as JSON (replaces the deprecated rewind --list).

Optionally filter condensed checkpoints by session ID with --session
(not applicable with --pending).

Usage:
  entire checkpoint list [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for list
      --json             Output as JSON instead of the human view
      --no-pager         Disable pager output
      --pending          List pending checkpoints — live shadow-branch state plus logs-only resume points
      --session string   Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

You can create an AI Search index using the UI, the Python SDK, or the REST API. The UI is the simplest approach.

There are two types of indexes:

  * Delta Sync Index automatically syncs with a source Delta Table, automatically and incrementally updating the index as the underlying data in the Delta Table changes.
  * Direct Vector Access Index supports direct read and write of vectors and metadata. The user is responsible for updating this table using the REST API or the Python SDK. This type of index cannot be created using the UI. You must use the REST API or the SDK.

Delta Sync Indexes support the following search modes:

  * Vector search (ANN or hybrid): Requires embedding columns. Supports both standard and storage-optimized endpoints. You can also use `query_type="FULL_TEXT"` for keyword search on these indexes.
  * Dedicated full-text search index (Beta): A Delta Sync Index created without any embedding columns, for keyword-only search. Available only on storage-optimized endpoints using triggered sync mode. See Create a full-text search index.

note

The column name `_id` is reserved. If your source table has a column named `_id`, rename it before creating an AI Search index.

### Create index using the UI​

  1. In the left sidebar, click Catalog to open the Catalog Explorer UI.

  2. Navigate to the Delta table you want to use.

  3. Click the Create button at the upper-right, and select Vector search index from the drop-down menu.

Image: Create index button

  4. Use the selectors in the dialog to configure the index.

Image: create index dialog

## Update an AI Search index​

### Update a Delta Sync Index​

Indexes created with Continuous sync mode automatically update when the source Delta table changes. If you are using Triggered sync mode, you can start the sync using the UI, the Python SDK, or the REST API.

  * Databricks UI
  * Python SDK
  * REST API

  1. In Catalog Explorer, navigate to the AI Search index.

  2. On the Overview tab, in the Data Ingest section, click Sync now.

Image: Sync now button to sync an AI Search index from Catalog Explorer..

For details, see the Python SDK reference.

Python
    
    `client = AISearchClient()
    index = client.get_index(index_name="vector_search_demo.vector_search.en_wiki_index")
    index.sync()
    `

See the REST API reference documentation: POST /api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/{index_name}/sync.

### Update a Direct Vector Access Index​

You can use the Python SDK or the REST API to insert, update, or delete data from a Direct Vector Access Index.

  * Python SDK
  * REST API

For details, see the Python SDK reference.

Python
    
    `index.upsert([
        {
            "id": 1,
            "field2": "value2",
            "field3": 3.0,
            "text_vector": [1.0] * 1024
        },
        {
            "id": 2,
            "field2": "value2",
            "field3": 3.0,
            "text_vector": [1.1] * 1024
        }
    ])
    `

See the REST API reference documentation: POST /api/2.0/vector-search/indexes.

For production applications, Databricks recommends using service principals instead of personal access tokens. Performance can be improved by up to 100 msec per query.

The following code example illustrates how to update an index using a service principal.

sh
    
    `export SP_CLIENT_ID=...
    export SP_CLIENT_SECRET=...
    export INDEX_NAME=...
    export WORKSPACE_URL=https://...
    export WORKSPACE_ID=...
    # Set authorization details to generate OAuth token
    export AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS='{"type":"unity_catalog_permission","securable_type":"table","securable_object_name":"'"$INDEX_NAME"'","operation": "WriteVectorIndex"}'
    # Generate OAuth token
    export TOKEN=$(curl -X POST --url $WORKSPACE_URL/oidc/v1/token -u "$SP_CLIENT_ID:$SP_CLIENT_SECRET" --data 'grant_type=client_credentials' --data 'scope=all-apis' --data-urlencode 'authorization_details=['"$AUTHORIZATION_DETAILS"']' | jq .access_token | tr -d '"')
    # Get index URL
    export INDEX_URL=$(curl -X GET -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME | jq -r '.status.index_url' | tr -d '"')
    # Upsert data into AI Search index.
    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url https://$INDEX_URL/upsert-data --data '{"inputs_json": "[...]"}'
    # Delete data from AI Search index
    curl -X DELETE -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url https://$INDEX_URL/delete-data --data '{"primary_keys": [...]}'
    `

The following code example illustrates how to update an index using a personal access token (PAT).

sh
    
    `export TOKEN=...
    export INDEX_NAME=...
    export WORKSPACE_URL=https://...
    # Upsert data into AI Search index.
    curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME/upsert-data --data '{"inputs_json": "..."}'
    # Delete data from AI Search index
    curl -X DELETE -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --url $WORKSPACE_URL/api/2.0/vector-search/indexes/$INDEX_NAME/delete-data --data '{"primary_keys": [...]}'
    `

### How to make schema changes with no downtime​

Schema changes to the source table are not supported unless you rebuild the index. This includes modifying existing columns and adding new columns. The index schema is fixed at creation time, so any schema changes require creating a new index to take effect.

Follow these steps to rebuild and deploy the index with no downtime:

  1. Perform the schema change on your source table.
  2. Create a new index using the updated schema.
  3. After the new index is ready, switch traffic to the new index.
  4. Delete the original index.

(file: r2/browser-use/0.1.0-alpha2/skills/browser/SKILL.md)

Use when the user asks "is this on brand", "check this against our brand kit", "do a brand review", "does this match our brand guidelines", or "brand-check my design". (file: r4/canva-brand-check/SKILL.md)

Use when the user asks to create a branded presentation, make an on-brand deck, turn an outline into slides, or generate a presentation from a brief. (file: r4/canva-branded-presentation/SKILL.md)

Accepts any tabular data source — uploaded files, pasted tables, JSON, or URLs. (file: r4/canva-bulk-create/SKILL.md)

Read-only; makes no changes to the design. Use when the user asks to "review my design", "give me feedback on this", "critique my deck/poster/flyer", "how can I improve this design", or "what's wrong with this slide". (file: r4/canva-design-feedback/SKILL.md)
- canva:canva-edit-design: Make edits to an existing Canva design — change or fix text, replace/insert/delete images and videos, reformat text (size, weight, style, color, alignment, lists, line height), reposition or resize elements, and update the title. Use when the user wants to change, edit, update, fix, translate, replace, or reformat content in a specific Canva design. This is the safe edit engine that other Canva skills (e.g. implement-feedback) build on. (file: r4/canva-edit-design/SKILL.md)
- canva:canva-implement-feedback: Implement reviewer feedback on a Canva design. Use when the user asks to "implement feedback on my deck", "address comments on a design", "apply review feedback", "fix the comments on my presentation", or "implement the feedback". (file: r4/canva-implement-feedback/SKILL.md)
- canva:canva-resize-for-social-media: Resize a Canva design into multiple social media formats (Facebook post, Facebook story, Instagram post, Instagram story, LinkedIn post). (file: r4/canva-resize-for-social-media/SKILL.md)

(file: r0/codex-computer-use/SKILL.md)
- codex-in-app-browser: Drive the Codex in-app browser (open, navigate, click, type, screenshot, read page state) through the app's own node_repl runtime. Use when the session uses a custom (non-OpenAI) model, for example deepseek-v4-flash or mimo-v2.5, and the user asks to use the in-app browser, open or navigate a page in it, test a local app in a browser, or click, type, or take a screenshot in the Codex browser panel. (file: r0/codex-in-app-browser/SKILL.md)
- codex-router: Orientation for custom (non-OpenAI) models running in the Codex app through the codex-router proxy. Explains that the app's native tools arrive as flattened codex_app__ and mcp__ names, that the router restores them so the app executes them, which companion skills to read before threads, browser, or computer-use work, and that a turn with no tool call ends the task. Use when the session uses a custom (non-OpenAI) model, for example deepseek-v4-flash or mimo-v2.5, when codex_app__ or mcp__ tool names appear in the tool list, when a tool result just arrived and more work remains, or when thread, browser, or computer-use work is requested. (file: r0/codex-router/SKILL.md)
- codex-router-media: Generate video, music, speech, or images with the operator's MiniMax Token Plan subscription through the codex-router media CLI. Use when the session runs a MiniMax custom (non-OpenAI) model (for example minimax-m3) with the MiniMax Token Plan provider connected, and the user explicitly asks to create a video, a song or music track, spoken audio, or an image. Do not use for reading or analyzing existing media. (file: r0/codex-router-media/SKILL.md)

(file: r6/google-drive/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-drive-comments: Write, reply to, and resolve Google Drive comments on Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Drive files with evidence-backed location context. Use when the user asks to leave comments, review a file with comments, respond to comment threads, or resolve Drive comments. (file: r6/google-drive-comments/SKILL.md)

(file: r6/google-sheets/SKILL.md)

(file: r5/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
